paper.abstract:
Abstract Bayesian optimization uses posterior uncertainty to decide where to
explore, but this uncertainty is not spatially neutral. On bounded
domains, Gaussian-process posterior variance is typically larger near faces, edges, and corners, giving variance-based acquisition functions a systematic boundary bias. This spatial preference is usually inherited from the surrogate rather than chosen as part of the exploration strategy.
We separate these roles by keeping the predictive model fixed and
modifying the spatial preference of the exploration term. We control the preference with spatial weight fields and amortize their construction with neural surrogates. Controlled experiments show that the Gaussian process’ default boundary bias changes which parts of the domain are explored and which optima are
reached.
We compare three alternative exploration principles and find, across standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks,
that they can often lower regret, particularly early in the optimization.
The spatial structure of posterior uncertainty is therefore not a
neutral default: it shapes the exploration strategy and can materially
affect optimization performance.

sections.heading: 1 INTRODUCTION
sections.text: Figure 1: A Gaussian process fitted on a bounded domain (top) and its posterior standard deviation (bottom). In this example, uncertainty is highest near the domain boundaries, so pure variance exploration selects a boundary point despite the larger gap between observations in the interior. In Gaussian-process (GP) Bayesian optimization ( Garnett, 2023 ) (BO), posterior uncertainty influences both how much to explore and where that exploration is directed. The overall strength of exploration is controlled by the acquisition function’s exploration weight, while its spatial preference is inherited from the GP posterior. On bounded domains, posterior variance is typically larger near faces, edges, and corners, producing a systematic boundary bias in variance-based exploration ( Figure 1 ; Siivola et al., 2018 ; Bånkestad et al., 2026 ). This boundary bias is not inherently beneficial or harmful—exploring the boundary helps when the optimum lies there. Standard BO, however, inherits it from the GP surrogate regardless of whether it is appropriate for the optimization problem. We therefore suggest complementing the familiar question of how much to explore with asking where to explore. Previous work has addressed spatial effects in Bayesian optimization, including methods for reducing boundary-seeking behavior ( Siivola et al., 2018 ; Oh et al., 2018 ) . In Bayesian experimental design, Jarl et al. (2026) proposed a geometric equalizer that removes the expected spatial variation of GP uncertainty without changing the predictive model. Here we extend this idea to BO by treating the spatial preference of variance-based exploration as a design choice. We introduce a spatial weight on the exploration term, compare three principles for defining it, and learn reusable weight fields for efficient use during optimization. We isolate this effect in a controlled landscape with local minima at different spatial locations, changing only which minimum is global. This allows us to test how the spatial preference of exploration affects which regions BO reaches. The default rule favors corner minima, whereas alternative spatial preferences more often reach face and interior minima. Similar differences appear on standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks, where spatial weighting often reduces regret early in the optimization.

Bayesian optimization primarily targets settings where observations are costly to acquire. To choose the next evaluation, it combines a predictive model (the GP) with an acquisition function α : Ω → ℝ \alpha:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} that scores candidate locations 𝒙 {\bm{x}} . On bounded domains, uncertainty is often higher near the boundary because locations there have fewer neighboring observations within the domain that can reduce it; Figure 2 illustrates this effect. Figure 2: Near edges and corners, fewer observations lie within the effective correlation neighborhood, leading to higher posterior uncertainty. Several methods have addressed related boundary effects by changing the predictive model or its geometry. Siivola et al. (2018) introduce virtual derivative-sign observations under an interior-optimum assumption, while BOCK ( Oh et al., 2018 ) replaces the kernel geometry with a cylindrical representation that reduces boundary attraction. Input transformations provide another way to alter the geometry seen by the surrogate ( Snoek et al., 2014 ; Doumont et al., 2026 ) . In these approaches, changes in exploration behavior are coupled to changes in the predictive model or its geometry. Spatial preferences can also be introduced directly through the acquisition function. π \pi BO ( Hvarfner et al., 2022 ) reweights the acquisition using a user-specified prior over the location of the optimum. In contrast, the preference studied here arises from the surrogate uncertainty itself, and we modify only the exploration term.

sections.heading: 2.1 Alternative Exploration Principles
sections.text: Local posterior variance is not the only way to decide where an observation is useful. In optimal experimental design and active learning, a candidate can instead be valued by how much it is expected to reduce uncertainty about the model or its predictions ( MacKay, 1992 ; Cohn et al., 1996 ) . For Gaussian processes, integrated variance reduction makes this idea explicit by favoring points whose observation reduces posterior uncertainty over a large part of the domain, even when their local variance is not maximal. Information-theoretic BO applies a related principle to information about the optimizer ( Hennig and Schuler, 2012 ; Hernández-Lobato et al., 2014 ) , while prediction-oriented active learning targets information about predictions in a region of interest ( Bickford Smith et al., 2023 ) . This suggests an alternative exploration principle: favor locations expected to reduce uncertainty elsewhere. A different principle is to maximize spatial coverage. Minimax and maximin designs promote coverage and separation ( Johnson et al., 1990 ) ; Latin-hypercube designs are widely used for computer experiments ( Morris and Mitchell, 1995 ) ; and low-discrepancy sequences such as scrambled Sobol points provide approximately uniform coverage of the domain ( Sobol’, 1967 ; Owen, 1998 ) . These methods target coverage of the accumulated design, whereas our uniform-allocation principle targets the distribution of the next pure-exploration selection.

sections.heading: 3 METHODS
sections.text: Standard GP-based BO uses the same posterior for prediction and exploration, but these roles need not be coupled. In Bayesian experimental design, Jarl et al. (2026) showed that the GP’s boundary bias can be modified while leaving the predictive model unchanged. We adopt the same separation in Bayesian optimization and treat the spatial preference of exploration as a design choice.

sections.heading: 3.5 Amortized Weight Fields
sections.text: Recomputing the weight fields as N N and ℓ \ell change during BO would be expensive. We therefore train principle-specific neural surrogates for each problem dimension D D over a range of ( N , ℓ ) (N,\ell) . Training can be done offline because the fields depend on 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , N N , ℓ \ell , and D D , but not on the observed values or on the realized BO design. During optimization, the trained surrogate is fixed and is evaluated at the current N N and chosen exploration lengthscale. The neural representation also provides gradients with respect to 𝐱 \mathbf{x} when optimizing the acquisition function. Each surrogate takes ( 𝐱 , N , ℓ ) (\mathbf{x},N,\ell) as input. The weight fields are invariant to reflections about the center of each coordinate axis and to permutations of the axes, so we encode these symmetries directly in the architecture. Each coordinate is transformed as δ j = 2 ​ x j ​ ( 1 − x j ) , \delta_{j}=2x_{j}(1-x_{j}), (13) which is unchanged under x j ↦ 1 − x j x_{j}\mapsto 1-x_{j} . The transformed coordinates are passed through a shared encoder and summed, making the output invariant to permutations of the coordinate axes. The surrogates approximate the quantities used to construct the three weight fields. Their training targets, calibration procedures, architectures, training ranges, Monte Carlo sample counts, and numerical validation are given in the appendix.

sections.heading: 4 RESULTS
sections.text: We first use a controlled synthetic landscape to isolate how spatial weighting changes where BO searches and which optimum it reaches. We then test whether the same effects appear on standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks.

sections.heading: 4.1 Spatial Preferences Change Where BO Explores
sections.text: We first consider the synthetic objective function in Figure 4 . It has minima with identical local shape on a weak periodic background: one near a corner, one near a face, one in the interior, and, for D ≥ 3 D\geq 3 , one near an edge. (The precise definition is given in Appendix C .) The boundary minima are at the same distance from their nearest wall and differ in the number of walls they touch. All four have the same objective value except the designated global minimum, which is lower. By changing only which minimum is global, we can test whether the spatial preference favors different parts of the domain. Figure 4: The controlled landscape in D = 2 D=2 , with local minima of identical shape near a corner, a face, and the interior. One minimum is made deeper and serves as the global minimum. Circles mark the neighborhoods used to determine whether each minimum is reached, and dotted lines separate the spatial classes used to categorize evaluation locations. We compare the default unweighted rule with the three alternative exploration rules at a fixed exploration lengthscale. The four methods thus differ only in terms of their weight fields. In Figure 5 , we report results for λ = 4 \lambda=4 , for which the exploration term changes the selected location in about half of the BO rounds. We use 25 25 paired seeds for each combination of dimension and global-minimum location, shared across the four exploration rules. Budgets, results for the remaining values of λ \lambda , and standard GP-LCB as a practical reference are given in Appendix C . Figure 5: Effect of the spatial exploration preference on sampling and optimization. Each row shows one dimension, with λ = 4 \lambda=4 and 25 25 paired seeds. Left: fraction of the first D + 2 D+2 evaluations after the initial design that fall in the interior, on a face, on an edge, or near a corner, together with the corresponding fraction of domain volume in grey. Whiskers are 90 % 90\% bootstrap intervals over seeds and the vertical axis is logarithmic. Right: simple regret per BO round for each location of the optimum, shown as the mean with 90 % 90\% confidence bands. Vertical dotted lines mark t = D + 2 t=D+2 and t = 2 ​ ( D + 2 ) t=2(D+2) . We first record where the first D + 2 D+2 evaluations of each run fall, grouping points by whether they lie in the interior or near one, two, or more walls, and compare these shares with the corresponding share of domain volume ( Figure 5 , left). The unweighted rule strongly prefers corners. In D = 3 D=3 , corners make up only 2.5 % 2.5\% of the domain but receive 60 % 60\% of the first five evaluations, while the interior occupies 35 % 35\% of the domain and receives 2 % 2\% . The corner share increases with dimension, from 55 % 55\% in D = 2 D=2 to 72 % 72\% in D = 4 D=4 . The three spatially weighted rules are much closer to the domain volume, with g uniform g_{\mathrm{uniform}} closest to uniform allocation and g eff g_{\mathrm{eff}} shifted somewhat toward the interior. This pattern is unchanged by which minimum is global, consistent with it arising from the exploration term rather than the objective. These differences in spatial allocation affect how often the rules reach minima in different parts of the domain. For each placement of the global minimum, we record whether a run enters a predefined neighborhood around it within the budget ( Tables 2 and 2 in Appendix C ). When the global minimum is at a corner, the unweighted rule reaches it much more often than the spatially weighted rules ( 83 % 83\% versus 17 17 – 33 % 33\% in D = 3 D=3 ). When it lies on a face or in the interior, the pattern reverses; for the interior minimum in D = 3 D=3 , the corresponding rates are 19 % 19\% and 50 50 – 69 % 69\% . The edge case lies between these two patterns. Tasks are ordered by the distance of the optimum to the boundary, with the dimension beside the name; the two robot-pushing simulators are shown to the right of the divider. Points are means over 100 100 paired seeds, with 90 % 90\% bootstrap intervals over the paired differences. All rules use λ = 2 \lambda=2 and the same exploration lengthscale. Beale, which every rule solves to zero regret, is omitted. Figure 5 , right, shows how these differences in discovery translate into simple regret. Early in the run, the spatially weighted rules have lower regret whenever the optimum is not in a corner and, in D = 3 D=3 and 4 4 , even in the corner case, by about 1 1 – 3 3 standardized objective units. The corner case also shows that reaching the correct region first is not the same as resolving the optimum. The unweighted rule enters the corner region early, but its evaluations concentrate on the corners themselves, where the objective remains above the nearby minimum. It then continues to other corners before refining the most promising one. By the end of the budget, the pattern has changed. The unweighted rule performs best when the optimum is in a corner, whereas the spatially weighted rules retain lower regret for face and interior optima and, in D = 4 D=4 , for the edge optimum as well. The spatial preference of exploration therefore affects both which optimum regions are found first and how much early regret is accumulated before they are refined. The differences increase with λ \lambda and are negligible at λ = 1 \lambda=1 , where all four rules are nearly greedy, consistent with the effect originating in the exploration term.

sections.heading: 4.2 Spatial Preferences Affect Benchmark Performance
sections.text: We next test whether the spatial effects observed in the controlled experiment also appear on standard benchmarks. We use nine synthetic functions in two to six dimensions and two stochastic robot-pushing simulators in 3D and 4D ( Wang and Jegelka, 2017 ) . Most optima lie in the interior, while Hartmann 3D, Hartmann 6D, and the 4D simulator have optima closer to the boundary. We compare the same four exploration rules at a common exploration lengthscale, using λ = 2 \lambda=2 and 100 100 paired seeds. Figure 6 reports regret relative to the unweighted rule after 2 ​ ( D + 2 ) 2(D+2) , 3 ​ ( D + 2 ) 3(D+2) , and 4 ​ ( D + 2 ) 4(D+2) evaluations, normalized by the regret after the shared initial design. Full trajectories and additional baselines are given in Appendix D . Figure 7: Simple regret on six representative tasks. Curves show means over 100 100 paired seeds with 90 % 90\% confidence bands. The dotted line marks 2 ​ ( D + 2 ) 2(D+2) evaluations, and uniform random sampling is shown in grey. Full trajectories are given in Appendix D . After 2 ​ ( D + 2 ) 2(D+2) evaluations, all three weighted rules have lower regret than the unweighted rule on every task shown in Figure 6 . The difference ranges from less than 10 % 10\% of the initial regret on the lower-dimensional Hartmann functions to about 40 % 40\% on Styblinski–Tang. The controlled experiment suggests one mechanism for this early advantage: the unweighted rule allocates more evaluations to the boundary, whereas the weighted rules allocate more to the interior, where most benchmark optima lie. By 3 ​ ( D + 2 ) 3(D+2) and 4 ​ ( D + 2 ) 4(D+2) evaluations, the differences have largely disappeared on Hartmann 3D, Hartmann 4D, and Levy, but remain large on Styblinski–Tang and visible on Michalewicz and Hartmann 6D ( Figure 6 ). On Hartmann 6D, the weighted rules reach the region containing the global minimum earlier, while on Styblinski–Tang the separation persists through much of the run ( Figure 7 ). More generally, performance gaps can persist when early evaluations lead the rules into different regions, but tend to shrink once they reach the same region. The robot-pushing tasks show that the same spatial effects also appear in stochastic optimization problems. All four GP rules solve the 3D task within the budget, so their differences are mainly early. On the 4D task, however, the weighted rules have lower regret at every checkpoint and finish 19 19 – 23 % 23\% below the unweighted rule relative to the initial regret. The unweighted rule also allocates many evaluations to the box boundaries. Because the orientation variable is periodic, two of these boundaries correspond to the same physical pose. Boundary-seeking exploration can therefore be costly even when a box boundary is only an artifact of the parameterization. Levy shows the opposite late-stage behavior. The unweighted rule spends more evaluations near the boundary early, increasing regret at first but also reducing uncertainty there. The weighted rules postpone those evaluations and retain more boundary uncertainty later. Their early advantage therefore disappears, and the unweighted rule finishes marginally ahead. Michalewicz exposes a different limitation. With the common exploration lengthscale, all four rules, including g = 1 g=1 , finish close to uniform random sampling, while standard GP-LCB with the fitted lengthscale performs substantially better (Appendix D ). The common lengthscale is too large to resolve the function’s narrow structure, and spatial reweighting cannot correct this mismatch. Thus g g controls where exploration is directed, whereas the exploration lengthscale controls the scale at which uncertainty is resolved.

sections.heading: 5 DISCUSSION
sections.text: Our main result is that variance-based BO contains an implicit spatial exploration policy. On bounded domains, this often favors faces, edges, and corners, and our experiments show that this preference can affect which regions are reached and which optima are found. The important point is not that boundary exploration is inherently undesirable, but that this preference is usually inherited from the GP rather than chosen for the optimization problem. There is unlikely to be a universally best spatial preference. Our three principles provide problem-agnostic alternatives when no reliable prior over the optimum location is available. If such prior knowledge does exist, it can instead be used to favor particular parts of the domain. Methods such as π \pi BO ( Hvarfner et al., 2022 ) make this type of prior preference explicit by reweighting the acquisition function. Our setting is complementary: even without such prior information, the GP already induces a spatial preference through its uncertainty. Combining explicit prior beliefs with control of this surrogate-induced preference is a natural direction for future work. When little is known about the location of the optimum, uniform allocation provides a natural reference, but our results show that spatial neutrality and search efficiency are not the same objective. Geometric equalization and efficiency-oriented exploration can perform better while retaining structure in the GP uncertainty rather than forcing the next exploration location to be uniformly distributed. The Levy experiments also show that the differences between rules are not determined by iteration number alone. It depends on the remaining spatial structure of uncertainty: evaluations avoided near the boundary early can leave uncertainty there to be resolved later. Spatial weighting addresses only one aspect of exploration. On Michalewicz, changing g g cannot compensate for an exploration lengthscale that is too large to resolve the narrow structure of the objective. This separates two choices: g g controls where exploration is directed, while the exploration lengthscale controls the scale at which uncertainty is resolved. The present constructions also exploit the symmetry of a box domain; irregular, constrained, or periodic domains may require weight fields adapted to their geometry. We have focused on GP-LCB because its additive exploration term makes this separation explicit. Extending the same perspective to other acquisition functions is less direct, but would help clarify how surrogate-induced spatial preferences appear in methods such as Thompson sampling ( Thompson, 1933 ) and Log Noisy Expected Improvement ( Ament et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.text: Variance-based BO contains an implicit spatial exploration policy. By separating this policy from the predictive model, we show that changing where uncertainty is emphasized can alter where BO searches, which optima it finds, and its regret. The GP’s default preference can be useful near the boundary, while alternative preferences can improve search elsewhere, particularly early in optimization. The spatial preference of exploration should therefore be treated as an explicit design choice in BO rather than as an unexamined consequence of the surrogate model.

sections.heading: Normalization of the weight field.
sections.text: In the benchmark experiments, the normalizing average g ¯ N \bar{g}_{N} is taken over the evaluated points rather than over the domain. The reason is exploration strength. With the domain average, the weighted rules select points at which g / g ¯ N g/\bar{g}_{N} is 1.14 1.14 – 1.19 1.19 , because the boundary is downweighted while the average is fixed at one. At the same λ \lambda , they therefore apply a 15 15 – 20 % 20\% larger exploration term at their own selections than the unweighted rule, so that a comparison at equal λ \lambda mixes the spatial preference with the amount of exploration. Averaging over the evaluated points removes this difference. We identified the effect in a first set of runs with the domain average, which Figure 10 reports for comparison. The early checkpoints are unchanged. At the later checkpoints, the domain average costs slightly on Levy and gains slightly on Hartmann 3D and 4D. sections.text: On Levy 4D, the unweighted rule places 67 % 67\% of its first 12 12 selections within half a design spacing of a wall, compared with 27 % 27\% for the weighted rules. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.14696v1 [cs.LG] 10 Oct 2026 Understanding Hidden Spatial Preferences in Bayesian Optimization Maria Bånkestad Jens Sjölund Research Institutes of Sweden (RISE) Uppsala University Abstract Bayesian optimization uses posterior uncertainty to decide where to explore, but this uncertainty is not spatially neutral. On bounded domains, Gaussian-process posterior variance is typically larger near faces, edges, and corners, giving variance-based acquisition functions a systematic boundary bias. This spatial preference is usually inherited from the surrogate rather than chosen as part of the exploration strategy. We separate these roles by keeping the predictive model fixed and modifying the spatial preference of the exploration term. We control the preference with spatial weight fields and amortize their construction with neural surrogates. Controlled experiments show that the Gaussian process’ default boundary bias changes which parts of the domain are explored and which optima are reached. We compare three alternative exploration principles and find, across standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks, that they can often lower regret, particularly early in the optimization. The spatial structure of posterior uncertainty is therefore not a neutral default: it shapes the exploration strategy and can materially affect optimization performance. 1 INTRODUCTION Figure 1: A Gaussian process fitted on a bounded domain (top) and its posterior standard deviation (bottom). In this example, uncertainty is highest near the domain boundaries, so pure variance exploration selects a boundary point despite the larger gap between observations in the interior. In Gaussian-process (GP) Bayesian optimization ( Garnett, 2023 ) (BO), posterior uncertainty influences both how much to explore and where that exploration is directed. The overall strength of exploration is controlled by the acquisition function’s exploration weight, while its spatial preference is inherited from the GP posterior. On bounded domains, posterior variance is typically larger near faces, edges, and corners, producing a systematic boundary bias in variance-based exploration ( Figure 1 ; Siivola et al., 2018 ; Bånkestad et al., 2026 ). This boundary bias is not inherently beneficial or harmful—exploring the boundary helps when the optimum lies there. Standard BO, however, inherits it from the GP surrogate regardless of whether it is appropriate for the optimization problem. We therefore suggest complementing the familiar question of how much to explore with asking where to explore. Previous work has addressed spatial effects in Bayesian optimization, including methods for reducing boundary-seeking behavior ( Siivola et al., 2018 ; Oh et al., 2018 ) . In Bayesian experimental design, Jarl et al. (2026) proposed a geometric equalizer that removes the expected spatial variation of GP uncertainty without changing the predictive model. Here we extend this idea to BO by treating the spatial preference of variance-based exploration as a design choice. We introduce a spatial weight on the exploration term, compare three principles for defining it, and learn reusable weight fields for efficient use during optimization. We isolate this effect in a controlled landscape with local minima at different spatial locations, changing only which minimum is global. This allows us to test how the spatial preference of exploration affects which regions BO reaches. The default rule favors corner minima, whereas alternative spatial preferences more often reach face and interior minima. Similar differences appear on standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks, where spatial weighting often reduces regret early in the optimization. 2 BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK We consider Bayesian optimization of an unknown function f : Ω → ℝ f\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R} on the unit cube Ω = [ 0 , 1 ] D \Omega=[0,1]^{D} , given access only to noisy observations y = f ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) + ε y=f({\bm{x}})+\varepsilon , ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ n 2 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{n}^{2}) . As usual, we model the unknown function as a Gaussian process, f ∼ 𝒢 ​ 𝒫 ​ ( μ ⁡ ( 𝒙 ) , k ⁡ ( 𝒙 , 𝒙 ′ ) ) f\sim\mathcal{GP}(\mu({\bm{x}}),k({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime})) , with mean function μ \mu and covariance kernel k k . Given observations 𝒟 = { ( 𝒙 i , y i ) } i = 1 N \mathcal{D}=\{({\bm{x}}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} , the posterior covariance between any two points 𝒙 {\bm{x}} and 𝒙 ′ {\bm{x}}^{\prime} is ( Rasmussen and Williams, 2006 ) c ⁡ ( 𝒙 , 𝒙 ′ ) = k ⁡ ( 𝒙 , 𝒙 ′ ) − 𝒌 𝒙 ⊤ ​ ( K + σ n 2 ​ I ) − 1 ​ 𝒌 𝒙 ′ , c({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime})=k({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime})-{\bm{k}}_{\bm{x}}^{\top}(K+\sigma_{n}^{2}I)^{-1}{\bm{k}}_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}}, (1) where the matrix elements K i ​ j = k ⁡ ( 𝒙 i , 𝒙 j ) K_{ij}=k({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}) , and 𝒌 𝒙 = ( k ⁡ ( 𝒙 1 , 𝒙 ) , … , k ⁡ ( 𝒙 N , 𝒙 ) ) ⊤ {\bm{k}}_{\bm{x}}=(k({\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}),\ldots,k({\bm{x}}_{N},{\bm{x}}))^{\top} . In particular, the posterior variance at 𝒙 {\bm{x}} is the diagonal entry σ 2 ​ ( 𝒙 ) = c ⁡ ( 𝒙 , 𝒙 ) \sigma^{2}({\bm{x}})=c({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}) . Bayesian optimization primarily targets settings where observations are costly to acquire. To choose the next evaluation, it combines a predictive model (the GP) with an acquisition function α : Ω → ℝ \alpha:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} that scores candidate locations 𝒙 {\bm{x}} . Common acquisition functions include expected improvement ( Jones et al., 1998 ) and confidence-bound methods ( Srinivas et al., 2010 ) . For minimization, we focus on the lower-confidence-bound acquisition α N ​ ( 𝐱 ) = μ N ​ ( 𝐱 ) − λ ​ σ N ​ ( 𝐱 ) , \alpha_{N}(\mathbf{x})=\mu_{N}(\mathbf{x})-\lambda\,\sigma_{N}(\mathbf{x}), (2) where μ N ​ ( 𝐱 ) \mu_{N}(\mathbf{x}) and σ N ​ ( 𝐱 ) \sigma_{N}(\mathbf{x}) denote the GP posterior mean and standard deviation, respectively, and λ \lambda controls the strength of exploration relative to exploitation. Let X N = { 𝐱 i } i = 1 N X_{N}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote the current design, that is, the N N locations observed so far. For fixed kernel hyperparameters, σ N ​ ( 𝐱 ) \sigma_{N}(\mathbf{x}) depends on X N X_{N} , the kernel, and the noise model, but not on the observed function values (see, e.g., Krause et al. (2008) ). Consequently, spatial variation in posterior uncertainty induces a spatial preference in variance-based exploration ( Bånkestad et al., 2026 ) . On bounded domains, uncertainty is often higher near the boundary because locations there have fewer neighboring observations within the domain that can reduce it; Figure 2 illustrates this effect. Figure 2: Near edges and corners, fewer observations lie within the effective correlation neighborhood, leading to higher posterior uncertainty. Several methods have addressed related boundary effects by changing the predictive model or its geometry. Siivola et al. (2018) introduce virtual derivative-sign observations under an interior-optimum assumption, while BOCK ( Oh et al., 2018 ) replaces the kernel geometry with a cylindrical representation that reduces boundary attraction. Input transformations provide another way to alter the geometry seen by the surrogate ( Snoek et al., 2014 ; Doumont et al., 2026 ) . In these approaches, changes in exploration behavior are coupled to changes in the predictive model or its geometry. Spatial preferences can also be introduced directly through the acquisition function. π \pi BO ( Hvarfner et al., 2022 ) reweights the acquisition using a user-specified prior over the location of the optimum. In contrast, the preference studied here arises from the surrogate uncertainty itself, and we modify only the exploration term. 2.1 Alternative Exploration Principles Local posterior variance is not the only way to decide where an observation is useful. In optimal experimental design and active learning, a candidate can instead be valued by how much it is expected to reduce uncertainty about the model or its predictions ( MacKay, 1992 ; Cohn et al., 1996 ) . For Gaussian processes, integrated variance reduction makes this idea explicit by favoring points whose observation reduces posterior uncertainty over a large part of the domain, even when their local variance is not maximal. Information-theoretic BO applies a related principle to information about the optimizer ( Hennig and Schuler, 2012 ; Hernández-Lobato et al., 2014 ) , while prediction-oriented active learning targets information about predictions in a region of interest ( Bickford Smith et al., 2023 ) . This suggests an alternative exploration principle: favor locations expected to reduce uncertainty elsewhere. A different principle is to maximize spatial coverage. Minimax and maximin designs promote coverage and separation ( Johnson et al., 1990 ) ; Latin-hypercube designs are widely used for computer experiments ( Morris and Mitchell, 1995 ) ; and low-discrepancy sequences such as scrambled Sobol points provide approximately uniform coverage of the domain ( Sobol’, 1967 ; Owen, 1998 ) . These methods target coverage of the accumulated design, whereas our uniform-allocation principle targets the distribution of the next pure-exploration selection. 3 METHODS Standard GP-based BO uses the same posterior for prediction and exploration, but these roles need not be coupled. In Bayesian experimental design, Jarl et al. (2026) showed that the GP’s boundary bias can be modified while leaving the predictive model unchanged. We adopt the same separation in Bayesian optimization and treat the spatial preference of exploration as a design choice. 3.1 Controlling Spatial Preferences by Weighting To control the spatial preference of exploration, we introduce a weight field g : Ω → ℝ + g:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}_{+} that acts on the uncertainty term of the acquisition function: α g ​ ( 𝐱 ) = μ N ​ ( 𝐱 ) − λ ​ g ​ ( 𝐱 ) ​ σ N ​ ( 𝐱 ) . \alpha_{g}(\mathbf{x})=\mu_{N}(\mathbf{x})-\lambda\,g(\mathbf{x})\,\sigma_{N}(\mathbf{x}). We consider three principles for choosing the weight field: equalizing systematic spatial variation in expected uncertainty, making pure-exploration selections approximately uniform over the domain, and favoring locations whose uncertainty produces greater domain-wide uncertainty reduction. 3.2 Reference Designs and Expected Uncertainty Let X ~ N \widetilde{X}_{N} denote the first N N points of a randomized Sobol sequence on Ω \Omega . (11) Here, ℓ ^ N \hat{\ell}_{N} is the fitted predictive lengthscale and ℓ e \ell_{e} is the exploration lengthscale. The posterior mean is evaluated at ℓ ^ N \hat{\ell}_{N} , while both g g and the exploration uncertainty σ N \sigma_{N} are evaluated at ℓ e \ell_{e} . In the main comparisons, we hold ℓ e \ell_{e} fixed and vary only g g ; all other components of BO, including the predictive GP, hyperparameter fitting, initial design, exploration weight, and acquisition optimizer, are shared across methods. 3.5 Amortized Weight Fields Recomputing the weight fields as N N and ℓ \ell change during BO would be expensive. We therefore train principle-specific neural surrogates for each problem dimension D D over a range of ( N , ℓ ) (N,\ell) . Training can be done offline because the fields depend on 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , N N , ℓ \ell , and D D , but not on the observed values or on the realized BO design. During optimization, the trained surrogate is fixed and is evaluated at the current N N and chosen exploration lengthscale. The neural representation also provides gradients with respect to 𝐱 \mathbf{x} when optimizing the acquisition function. Each surrogate takes ( 𝐱 , N , ℓ ) (\mathbf{x},N,\ell) as input. The weight fields are invariant to reflections about the center of each coordinate axis and to permutations of the axes, so we encode these symmetries directly in the architecture. Each coordinate is transformed as δ j = 2 ​ x j ​ ( 1 − x j ) , \delta_{j}=2x_{j}(1-x_{j}), (13) which is unchanged under x j ↦ 1 − x j x_{j}\mapsto 1-x_{j} . The transformed coordinates are passed through a shared encoder and summed, making the output invariant to permutations of the coordinate axes. The surrogates approximate the quantities used to construct the three weight fields. Their training targets, calibration procedures, architectures, training ranges, Monte Carlo sample counts, and numerical validation are given in the appendix. 4 RESULTS We first use a controlled synthetic landscape to isolate how spatial weighting changes where BO searches and which optimum it reaches. We then test whether the same effects appear on standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks. 4.1 Spatial Preferences Change Where BO Explores We first consider the synthetic objective function in Figure 4 . It has minima with identical local shape on a weak periodic background: one near a corner, one near a face, one in the interior, and, for D ≥ 3 D\geq 3 , one near an edge. (The precise definition is given in Appendix C .) The boundary minima are at the same distance from their nearest wall and differ in the number of walls they touch. All four have the same objective value except the designated global minimum, which is lower. By changing only which minimum is global, we can test whether the spatial preference favors different parts of the domain. Figure 4: The controlled landscape in D = 2 D=2 , with local minima of identical shape near a corner, a face, and the interior. One minimum is made deeper and serves as the global minimum. Circles mark the neighborhoods used to determine whether each minimum is reached, and dotted lines separate the spatial classes used to categorize evaluation locations. We compare the default unweighted rule with the three alternative exploration rules at a fixed exploration lengthscale. The four methods thus differ only in terms of their weight fields. In Figure 5 , we report results for λ = 4 \lambda=4 , for which the exploration term changes the selected location in about half of the BO rounds. We use 25 25 paired seeds for each combination of dimension and global-minimum location, shared across the four exploration rules. Budgets, results for the remaining values of λ \lambda , and standard GP-LCB as a practical reference are given in Appendix C . Figure 5: Effect of the spatial exploration preference on sampling and optimization. Each row shows one dimension, with λ = 4 \lambda=4 and 25 25 paired seeds. Left: fraction of the first D + 2 D+2 evaluations after the initial design that fall in the interior, on a face, on an edge, or near a corner, together with the corresponding fraction of domain volume in grey. Whiskers are 90 % 90\% bootstrap intervals over seeds and the vertical axis is logarithmic. Right: simple regret per BO round for each location of the optimum, shown as the mean with 90 % 90\% confidence bands. Vertical dotted lines mark t = D + 2 t=D+2 and t = 2 ​ ( D + 2 ) t=2(D+2) . We first record where the first D + 2 D+2 evaluations of each run fall, grouping points by whether they lie in the interior or near one, two, or more walls, and compare these shares with the corresponding share of domain volume ( Figure 5 , left). The unweighted rule strongly prefers corners. In D = 3 D=3 , corners make up only 2.5 % 2.5\% of the domain but receive 60 % 60\% of the first five evaluations, while the interior occupies 35 % 35\% of the domain and receives 2 % 2\% . The corner share increases with dimension, from 55 % 55\% in D = 2 D=2 to 72 % 72\% in D = 4 D=4 . The three spatially weighted rules are much closer to the domain volume, with g uniform g_{\mathrm{uniform}} closest to uniform allocation and g eff g_{\mathrm{eff}} shifted somewhat toward the interior. This pattern is unchanged by which minimum is global, consistent with it arising from the exploration term rather than the objective. These differences in spatial allocation affect how often the rules reach minima in different parts of the domain. For each placement of the global minimum, we record whether a run enters a predefined neighborhood around it within the budget ( Tables 2 and 2 in Appendix C ). When the global minimum is at a corner, the unweighted rule reaches it much more often than the spatially weighted rules ( 83 % 83\% versus 17 17 – 33 % 33\% in D = 3 D=3 ). When it lies on a face or in the interior, the pattern reverses; for the interior minimum in D = 3 D=3 , the corresponding rates are 19 % 19\% and 50 50 – 69 % 69\% . The edge case lies between these two patterns. Tasks are ordered by the distance of the optimum to the boundary, with the dimension beside the name; the two robot-pushing simulators are shown to the right of the divider. Points are means over 100 100 paired seeds, with 90 % 90\% bootstrap intervals over the paired differences. All rules use λ = 2 \lambda=2 and the same exploration lengthscale. Beale, which every rule solves to zero regret, is omitted. Figure 5 , right, shows how these differences in discovery translate into simple regret. Early in the run, the spatially weighted rules have lower regret whenever the optimum is not in a corner and, in D = 3 D=3 and 4 4 , even in the corner case, by about 1 1 – 3 3 standardized objective units. The corner case also shows that reaching the correct region first is not the same as resolving the optimum. The unweighted rule enters the corner region early, but its evaluations concentrate on the corners themselves, where the objective remains above the nearby minimum. It then continues to other corners before refining the most promising one. By the end of the budget, the pattern has changed. The unweighted rule performs best when the optimum is in a corner, whereas the spatially weighted rules retain lower regret for face and interior optima and, in D = 4 D=4 , for the edge optimum as well. The spatial preference of exploration therefore affects both which optimum regions are found first and how much early regret is accumulated before they are refined. The differences increase with λ \lambda and are negligible at λ = 1 \lambda=1 , where all four rules are nearly greedy, consistent with the effect originating in the exploration term. 4.2 Spatial Preferences Affect Benchmark Performance We next test whether the spatial effects observed in the controlled experiment also appear on standard benchmarks. We use nine synthetic functions in two to six dimensions and two stochastic robot-pushing simulators in 3D and 4D ( Wang and Jegelka, 2017 ) . Most optima lie in the interior, while Hartmann 3D, Hartmann 6D, and the 4D simulator have optima closer to the boundary. We compare the same four exploration rules at a common exploration lengthscale, using λ = 2 \lambda=2 and 100 100 paired seeds. Figure 6 reports regret relative to the unweighted rule after 2 ​ ( D + 2 ) 2(D+2) , 3 ​ ( D + 2 ) 3(D+2) , and 4 ​ ( D + 2 ) 4(D+2) evaluations, normalized by the regret after the shared initial design. Full trajectories and additional baselines are given in Appendix D . Figure 7: Simple regret on six representative tasks. Curves show means over 100 100 paired seeds with 90 % 90\% confidence bands. The dotted line marks 2 ​ ( D + 2 ) 2(D+2) evaluations, and uniform random sampling is shown in grey. Full trajectories are given in Appendix D . After 2 ​ ( D + 2 ) 2(D+2) evaluations, all three weighted rules have lower regret than the unweighted rule on every task shown in Figure 6 . The difference ranges from less than 10 % 10\% of the initial regret on the lower-dimensional Hartmann functions to about 40 % 40\% on Styblinski–Tang. The controlled experiment suggests one mechanism for this early advantage: the unweighted rule allocates more evaluations to the boundary, whereas the weighted rules allocate more to the interior, where most benchmark optima lie. By 3 ​ ( D + 2 ) 3(D+2) and 4 ​ ( D + 2 ) 4(D+2) evaluations, the differences have largely disappeared on Hartmann 3D, Hartmann 4D, and Levy, but remain large on Styblinski–Tang and visible on Michalewicz and Hartmann 6D ( Figure 6 ). On Hartmann 6D, the weighted rules reach the region containing the global minimum earlier, while on Styblinski–Tang the separation persists through much of the run ( Figure 7 ). More generally, performance gaps can persist when early evaluations lead the rules into different regions, but tend to shrink once they reach the same region. The robot-pushing tasks show that the same spatial effects also appear in stochastic optimization problems. All four GP rules solve the 3D task within the budget, so their differences are mainly early. On the 4D task, however, the weighted rules have lower regret at every checkpoint and finish 19 19 – 23 % 23\% below the unweighted rule relative to the initial regret. The unweighted rule also allocates many evaluations to the box boundaries. Because the orientation variable is periodic, two of these boundaries correspond to the same physical pose. Boundary-seeking exploration can therefore be costly even when a box boundary is only an artifact of the parameterization. Levy shows the opposite late-stage behavior. The unweighted rule spends more evaluations near the boundary early, increasing regret at first but also reducing uncertainty there. The weighted rules postpone those evaluations and retain more boundary uncertainty later. Their early advantage therefore disappears, and the unweighted rule finishes marginally ahead. Michalewicz exposes a different limitation. With the common exploration lengthscale, all four rules, including g = 1 g=1 , finish close to uniform random sampling, while standard GP-LCB with the fitted lengthscale performs substantially better (Appendix D ). The common lengthscale is too large to resolve the function’s narrow structure, and spatial reweighting cannot correct this mismatch. Thus g g controls where exploration is directed, whereas the exploration lengthscale controls the scale at which uncertainty is resolved. 5 DISCUSSION Our main result is that variance-based BO contains an implicit spatial exploration policy. On bounded domains, this often favors faces, edges, and corners, and our experiments show that this preference can affect which regions are reached and which optima are found. The important point is not that boundary exploration is inherently undesirable, but that this preference is usually inherited from the GP rather than chosen for the optimization problem. There is unlikely to be a universally best spatial preference. Our three principles provide problem-agnostic alternatives when no reliable prior over the optimum location is available. If such prior knowledge does exist, it can instead be used to favor particular parts of the domain. Methods such as π \pi BO ( Hvarfner et al., 2022 ) make this type of prior preference explicit by reweighting the acquisition function. Our setting is complementary: even without such prior information, the GP already induces a spatial preference through its uncertainty. Combining explicit prior beliefs with control of this surrogate-induced preference is a natural direction for future work. When little is known about the location of the optimum, uniform allocation provides a natural reference, but our results show that spatial neutrality and search efficiency are not the same objective. Geometric equalization and efficiency-oriented exploration can perform better while retaining structure in the GP uncertainty rather than forcing the next exploration location to be uniformly distributed. The Levy experiments also show that the differences between rules are not determined by iteration number alone. It depends on the remaining spatial structure of uncertainty: evaluations avoided near the boundary early can leave uncertainty there to be resolved later. Spatial weighting addresses only one aspect of exploration. On Michalewicz, changing g g cannot compensate for an exploration lengthscale that is too large to resolve the narrow structure of the objective. This separates two choices: g g controls where exploration is directed, while the exploration lengthscale controls the scale at which uncertainty is resolved. The present constructions also exploit the symmetry of a box domain; irregular, constrained, or periodic domains may require weight fields adapted to their geometry. We have focused on GP-LCB because its additive exploration term makes this separation explicit. Extending the same perspective to other acquisition functions is less direct, but would help clarify how surrogate-induced spatial preferences appear in methods such as Thompson sampling ( Thompson, 1933 ) and Log Noisy Expected Improvement ( Ament et al., 2023 ) . 6 CONCLUSION Variance-based BO contains an implicit spatial exploration policy. By separating this policy from the predictive model, we show that changing where uncertainty is emphasized can alter where BO searches, which optima it finds, and its regret. The GP’s default preference can be useful near the boundary, while alternative preferences can improve search elsewhere, particularly early in optimization. The spatial preference of exploration should therefore be treated as an explicit design choice in BO rather than as an unexamined consequence of the surrogate model.
